components.text: Whether the proposed whole-worldview method permits progress through comparison of primitive commitments at reality's roots.
Whether comparative progress must await fully developed worldviews rather than beginning at their fundamental roots.
Whether naturalness is best treated as a universally instantiated category rather than a historically restricted contrast class.
Whether natural should be treated as a universally instantiated category rather than a historically restricted one.
Whether historical restricted usage should govern the substantive categorical relation between the foundation and other concrete things.
Whether inherited natural and supernatural labels establish a categorical discontinuity between foundation and created reality.
Whether the theistic foundation shares a broad concrete category with created reality despite being uncreated.
Whether the proposed theistic foundation uniquely avoids abrupt categorical separation from later concrete reality.
Whether naturalistic initial reality possesses broad physical and temporal continuity with the later manifold.
Whether a necessary naturalistic initial reality is physically and temporally continuous with what follows.
Whether attributing mentality follows from merely removing arbitrary limits rather than adding a positive property.
Whether attributing consciousness follows from removing arbitrary limits rather than adding a positive property.
Whether removing value limitations can yield a positive supreme foundation without multiplying fundamental commitments.
Whether positive attributes can be derived from removing a limit rather than introduced as independent structure.
Whether the necessary initial reality must possess specifiable nonarbitrary limits and whether necessity can itself be called arbitrary.
Whether removing alleged arbitrary limits warrants a positive supreme characterization of the initial reality.
Whether necessary limits are arbitrary commitments that increase theoretical complexity.
Whether removing alleged limits warrants a positive characterization of the initial reality.
Whether necessary existence terminates all relevant explanation of the initial reality's particular features.
Whether necessity terminates explanatory demand for the initial reality and its particular features.
Whether independent necessary domains lose explanatory value compared with derivation from a smaller unified basis.
Whether independent necessary domains lose explanatory value relative to derivation from a unified basis.
Whether eliminating arbitrary intermediate limits entails nonzero or unlimited consciousness and hence personhood.
Whether excluding intermediate value limits entails maximal consciousness or personhood.
Whether direct introspection can establish that consciousness is not identical with appropriately situated neural processing.
Whether direct introspective access to consciousness establishes its nonidentity with neural processing.
Whether experiential contents must be distinct from the neural processing whose contents are introspectively available.
Whether conscious content must be distinct from the neural processing that makes it available.
Whether identity of a conscious episode with a neural process entails reduction of every conscious property to a physical type.
Whether an identity theory can allow conscious and neural properties without strict type-level reduction.
Whether one neural process can be identical with consciousness while conscious properties remain irreducible to physical types.
Whether identity theory entails reduction of every introspectively available conscious aspect to a neural type.
Whether focused property-level analysis retains legitimate evidential value despite being insufficient to decide complete-worldview superiority.
Whether examining a selected local consideration is useful despite being insufficient for a complete-worldview verdict.
